newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine economy has several weak spots - bank.
newsitem.headline: Philippine economy has several weak spots - bank.

text.p: The Philippines would have to address several weak spots to ensure its long-term success inspite of the economic liberalisation programmes it had undertaken, economists of Far East Bank and Trust Co said in a briefing on Wednesday.

Policies would have to be focused on the country's low domestic savings rate; dependence on overseas workers' remittances, lack of physical infrastructure and low agricultural productivity, they said.

Emma Pante, chief economist at the bank, said the country's low domestic savings rate of around 15 percent of Gross Domestic Product versus its East Asian neighbours' 30 percent had made it heavily dependent on foreign capital and portfolio funds from abroad.
While remittances had improved savings, Pante said, "overdependence on overseas Filipino workers' remittances has its risks since it is vulnerable to external events."
She said infrastructure requirements of the country are estimated at $50 billion up to the year 2004.
The country's low farm output had barely kept up with population growth, she said.

"Comprising, almost one-fourth of GDP, the agricultural sector is important not only in terms of economic growth but also keeping inflation in check. The food, beverage and tobacco component accounts for almost 60 percent of the consumer price index - the barometer of the general price level," she said.
Ronald Antonio Butiong, the banks' senior manager, said the bank projected Gross National Product to rise to 7.0 to 7.7 percent in 1997 from an estimate of 7.2 in 1996.

The country's trade deficit is forecast to widen to $14.5 billion to $15.6 billion in 1997 from an estimate of $12.4 billion in 1996 on account of heavy purchases of capital equipment, including aircraft, he said.
Gross international reserves could rise to $14.0 to $14.5 billion this year from a projected $11.5 billion last year.

The overall balance of payments, could be a surplus within the wide range of $1.0 billion to $3.0 billion due to the highly volatile and unpredictable nature of foreign portfolio investments compared to the 1996 estimate of $4.0 billion, he said. -- Manila newsroom 63 2 841-8937 fax 8176267
